triples.head: plants
triples.evidence: Explain how plants absorb energy from sunlight

triples.head: photoautotrophs
triples.evidence: In the case of photosynthesis, light energy is converted into chemical energy, which photoautotrophs use to build basic carbohydrate molecules (Figure 8.9).

triples.head: photoautotrophs
triples.evidence: However, autotrophs only use a few specific wavelengths of sunlight.

triples.head: pigments
triples.evidence: Light energy initiates the process of photosynthesis when pigments absorb specific wavelengths of visible light.

triples.head: chlorophyll a
triples.tail: wavelengths from either end of the visible spectrum (blue and red)
triples.evidence: Chlorophyll a absorbs wavelengths from either end of the visible spectrum (blue and red), but not green.

triples.head: chlorophyll a
triples.evidence: Because green is reflected or transmitted, chlorophyll appears green.

triples.head: carotenoids
triples.evidence: Carotenoids absorb in the short-wavelength blue region, and reflect the longer yellow, red, and orange wavelengths.

triples.head: thylakoid membrane
triples.evidence: Chlorophyll a and b are found in higher plant chloroplasts and will be the focus of the following discussion.

triples.head: thylakoid membrane
triples.evidence: The carotenoids found in fruit—such as the red of tomato (lycopene), the yellow of corn seeds (zeaxanthin), or the orange of an orange peel (β-carotene)—are used as advertisements to attract seed dispersers.

triples.head: photosystem II
triples.evidence: In the photosystem II (PSII) reaction center, energy from sunlight is used to extract electrons from water.

triples.head: photosystem I
triples.evidence: The electrons travel through the chloroplast electron transport chain to photosystem I (PSI), which reduces NADP to NADPH.

triples.head: photosystem II
triples.evidence: Splitting one H2O molecule releases two electrons, two hydrogen atoms, and one atom of oxygen.

triples.head: photosystem II
triples.evidence: Splitting one H2O molecule releases two electrons, two hydrogen atoms, and one atom of oxygen.

triples.head: thylakoid lumen
triples.evidence: Those hydrogen atoms, plus the ones produced by splitting water, accumulate in the thylakoid lumen and will be used to synthesize ATP in a later step.

triples.head: ATP synthase
triples.tail: a third phosphate group to ADP
triples.evidence: The energy released by the hydrogen ion stream allows ATP synthase to attach a third phosphate group to ADP, which forms a molecule of ATP (Figure 8.17).
